json.summary: A truck driver discovers that someone is lying on the flatbed and demands to know what he is doing there. The hidden man claims that he was injured by two large shopping bags on Gubacs Teréz Street, but his story keeps changing from last Tuesday to last week Tuesday, making the driver increasingly furious. The running gag is that the injured man is treated like something the truck has picked up, while the truck’s absurdly mangled signs and repeated phone number suggest a bizarre collection service.

characters.name: truck driver
characters.description: A stocky, middle-aged man with a large nose, heavy-lidded eyes, braided hair and a work vest/backpack. He is loud, impatient and highly profane, using colloquial Hungarian swearing and repeated 'bazme(g)' interjections; his speech is incredulous, confrontational and increasingly exasperated.

characters.name: injured man on the flatbed
characters.description: A mostly unseen man lying on or inside the truck’s flatbed, later associated with the blanket visible there. He speaks in a flat, plaintive, slightly incoherent way, repeatedly reporting pain and giving an implausible account of how he got there; his groans are exaggerated and his speech is less profane than the driver’s.

panels.description: A small work truck moves across the panel while the truck driver hurries beside it; a person’s legs protrude from the truck area. The hidden injured man groans from the truck in r1, while the driver’s cry outside the boxed text is not editable; the truck carries a mangled service sign.

The truck is at left and the truck driver stands at right, looking toward whoever is lying on the flatbed. The injured man groans in r1, the driver asks what the hell is going on in r2, and the truck’s side repeats its phone-number slogan in r3.

The truck driver confronts the unseen man on the flatbed and asks who he is and what the hell he is looking for there. The injured man answers from the truck that he was hit on Gubacs Teréz Street and that both legs have hurt ever since; the truck also bears the absurd sign 'FEKSZEM ITT.'

The truck driver denies having been anywhere near the place that day, while the injured man calmly insists that the incident happened last Tuesday. A blank speech region r10 has no text, and the truck’s phone-number sign remains visible.

The driver angrily challenges the injured man’s claim that the event happened last Tuesday and asks how he could have survived without food. The injured man says that two large shopping bags hit him head-on while he was coming out of a shop, leaving the account deliberately ridiculous and incomplete; the phone-number wording appears again.
The truck driver reaches the limit of his patience and curses. The truck continues past with the repeated phone-number sign; r17 and r18 are empty regions with no dialogue or sound text.
Only the rear portion of the truck is shown as it moves away. The injured man gives another long groan from the truck, while the side again displays the phone-number wording.

The truck driver gestures toward the flatbed, where a blanket or bundled covering is now visible, and says that there is a blanket there because the nights are getting cold. The injured man is implied to be under or beside it; the truck’s phone-number sign remains unchanged.

notes: The central joke is that the truck driver treats the injured man as an inexplicable object lying on his flatbed, while the injured man presents himself like something that has been collected. The repeated truck wording 'FELVESZEM' can mean 'I will pick it up' as well as 'I will answer [the phone],' supporting the pickup/collection joke.
The driver’s 'MI A FASZOM?' literally means 'What is my dick?' but is a very common vulgar equivalent of 'What the fuck?' It establishes his aggressive, fed-up register.

'GECIT' literally refers to semen/cum, but in 'mi a gecit keresel' it is a vulgar intensifier meaning roughly 'what the fuck are you looking for.' 'BAZME?' is a clipped form of 'bazmeg,' literally an obscene sexual curse and pragmatically an exclamation like 'for fuck’s sake' or 'mate, seriously?' The clipped spelling keeps the rough, casual sound.

'NE KAMUZZÁ!' means 'Don’t bullshit me!' or literally 'Don’t lie/use bullshit on me.' 'AKURVA ÉLET!' is a fused, emphatic form of 'a kurva élet,' literally 'the whore’s life,' used like 'for fuck’s sake!' or 'goddamn it!' These should remain strongly vulgar in English.

The injured man’s account is intentionally malformed and unreliable. 'A GUBACS TERÉZ ÚTON ÜTÖTTEL' appears to evoke a place or street name, 'Gubacs Teréz,' together with 'úton' ('on the road/street') and the verb phrase 'ütött el' ('hit/knocked me down'), but the wording is run together as 'ütöttel'; preserve the confused, ungrammatical quality rather than normalizing it.

The injured man says 'MINDKÉT LÁBAM ELTÖRÖTT' ('both my legs broke/were broken') and then repeats 'FÁJ. FÁJOGAT.' 'Fáj' means 'it hurts'; 'fájogat' is a diminutive or iterative form suggesting 'it aches a bit/keeps hurting.' The bathos comes from his understated, repetitive complaint after an absurd accident.

The claim that two shopping bags ('két nagy szatyor') hit him 'telibe' ('straight on, full in the face/full force') while he was leaving a shop is an absurd parody of a road-accident report. 'Szatyor' means an ordinary shopping bag, not a dangerous vehicle, so the alleged injury is comically disproportionate.

The contradictory timing is a running gag: the driver says he was not there 'ma' ('today') and not even 'a közelbe' ('anywhere nearby') in r8, while the injured man says 'ez múlt hét kedden történt' ('this happened last Tuesday') in r9. The driver then repeats 'Múlt hét kedd?' ('Last Tuesday?') in r12, exposing how little sense the conversation makes.

The groans 'HRAHGHHRRR....' in r1 and 'AAAARRRGH....' in r19 are exaggerated pain noises from the injured man and should be rendered as ugly, prolonged comic groans rather than polished dialogue. Their occurrence in r1 and r19 frames the verbal exchange with a physical gag.

The injured man’s 'ITT EGY PLÉD' means 'Here’s a blanket,' and 'ÉJJELENTE MÁR HIDEGEK VANNAK' means 'It’s getting cold at night' or literally 'the nights are already cold.' 'Pléd' is an ordinary loanword for a blanket/throw; the sudden practical concern about bedding makes the supposed accident victim seem like a homeless person settling into the truck.

The truck’s signs are intentionally nonsensical or corrupted. In p0 r0 reads exactly 'ÉPÖIPAI KITTELEZÉS • OG'; it resembles a badly scrambled or miscopied industrial-service slogan and should be kept as drawn, without silently correcting it. Its unreadability contributes to the low-quality, absurd background world.

The sign 'FEKSZEM ITT.' in p2 r6 literally means 'I am lying here.' It is funny because it functions like a label for the man lying on the truck, or like an absurd truck slogan; keep the blunt wording and punctuation rather than explaining it in the artwork.

The recurring truck sign reads '7722.683/FELVESZEM' in p0 r3, p2 r7, p3 r11 and p7 r22; p4 r14 reads '7722·683/FELVESZEM,' while p5 r16 and p6 r20 read '7722 · 683/FELVESZEM.' 'FELVESZEM' literally means 'I pick it up' or 'I’ll pick up/answer [the phone],' so it is both a contact slogan and a joke about the truck picking up the injured man. Preserve the number and the varying dot spacing exactly; no explanation is needed inside the translated comic.

The sign regions r0, r3, r6, r7, r11, r14, r16, r20 and r22 are background lettering, not spoken dialogue. The detector labels r11, r14 and r20 as speech-like regions, but their visual function is still truck signage and they should be localized as signs.

There are no named characters in the strip. 'Gubacs Teréz' should not automatically be treated as the injured man’s name; in context it is part of his confused account of where the accident happened and may be a distorted street/place reference.

The strip relies on ordinary Hungarian urban details—shopping bags, leaving a shop, a work truck, a blanket for cold nights—and turns them into an absurd pseudo-emergency. No specific brand, celebrity or historical reference needs adaptation.
